articles.title_orig: China urges ensuring normal flow of key livelihood supplies in Black Sea
articles.title_zh: China urges ensuring normal flow of key livelihood supplies in Black Sea
articles.content_orig:
UNITED NATIONS – A Chinese envoy on Monday called for ensuring the normal flow of essential supplies for people's livelihoods in the Black Sea, as the Ukraine crisis continues to drag on and hostilities keep escalating.
The conflict has not only inflicted profound suffering on the parties concerned, but also triggered negative spillover effects across the region and beyond, said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations.
Both Russia and Ukraine are major global grain producers, and Russia is also a major supplier of oil and fertilizers. As an important waterway for the outbound shipment of goods from both countries, the Black Sea plays a vital role in global production and supply chains, he told a high-level meeting of the Security Council.
ALSO READ: Trilateral talks on Ukraine begin
For some time now, multiple attacks on merchant vessels have occurred in the Black Sea, and port facilities in both countries have also been damaged, disrupting grain and energy exports and causing fluctuations in global grain and oil prices, for which developing countries have paid a heavy price, he noted.
"We call for protecting the safety and security of civilian merchant vessels and port facilities, ensuring the normal flow of grain, oil and other essential supplies for people's livelihoods from both sides, and promoting global economic stability," said Fu.
A Cold War mentality, bloc politics, and division and confrontation do not help achieve a political settlement of the crisis. Only mutual respect, dialogue and negotiation, and openness and inclusiveness can bring the dawn of peace, he said.
READ MORE: Zelensky, US envoys discuss peace process
China welcomes the recent trilateral talks among Russia, Ukraine, and the United States, as well as interactions carried out by relevant parties to advance negotiations. China hopes all parties will demonstrate political will, maintain engagement and communication, take each other's legitimate security concerns seriously, properly address the root causes of the conflict, commit to reaching a comprehensive, lasting and binding peace agreement, promote the building of a balanced, effective and sustainable regional security architecture, and achieve long-term peace and stability in the region, he said.
China always stands on the side of peace and dialogue, advocates a ceasefire and cessation of hostilities, and strives to promote peace and talks. China stands ready to work with the international community and continue making unremitting efforts to achieve a political settlement of the crisis and maintain regional peace and stability, while playing a constructive role in mitigating the spillover effects of the crisis and promoting sustainable development, he said.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Commerce adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist
articles.content_orig:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title_orig: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
articles.title_zh: Amazon drone delivering shampoo snags on wire and tumbles onto Michigan man’s garage roof
articles.content_orig:
A drone making a delivery for the online retailer Amazon crashed outside of Detroit on Friday after delivering a bottle of shampoo and now the Federal Aviation Administration is investigating.
The uncrewed vehicle successfully delivered the package to Jim Brennan’s Huntington Woods, Michigan, backyard shortly after his wife placed the order, he told CNN affiliate WXYZ .
“She ordered shampoo, and we just expected a truck to pull up, and then we get the notifications it’s coming by drone in seven minutes,” Brennan said.
The package was left in the backyard, but as he watched the Prime Air drone taking off, it hit a fiberoptic cable and knocked off a propeller.
“All of a sudden I realized it’s under a wire. It’s going to come up under that wire. And it did. And when it caught that, it just, it went crazy,” he said. “Like a sick bird, it tried to get out of here, but it couldn’t.”
Video recorded by Claire Brennan, who is not related to Jim Brennan, shows the aircraft struggling to fly before wobbling out of control and crashing as she walked by.
The drone landed on Logan Coomes’ garage next door, which he said had some minor damage.
“There’s a little corner on the tip of the peak of the garage where I think if it did rain, water would get through right now,” he told WXYZ. “Some shingles were flapped up from their original positions.”
No one was injured in the crash, Amazon said in a statement to CNN. The company removed the damaged drone from Coomes’ garage and is in contact with him.
“Safety is our top priority and incidents are extremely rare,” Jack Stelzner, an Amazon spokesperson, said. “Anytime a delivery does not go as planned we investigate what happened and use the findings to further improve the service.”
Prime Air drones have delivered hundreds of thousands of packages this year and nearly 6,000 are flown a day, Amazon said.
The “highly autonomous” MK30 drones can deliver items weighing five pounds or less, including groceries, cosmetics, medicine and electronics to the area surrounding their bases, the company said.
Locations are limited, but in August Amazon announced plans to reach nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of the year, a six-fold increase. The company plans to reach half a billion customers a year by the end of the decade.
The MK30 drones are designed to have a “best-in-class perception system to detect and avoid obstacles,” according to the company, and “navigate around obstacles like trampolines or clotheslines that may not have been captured in satellite imagery.”
Still, there have been crashes.
Last fall, Amazon ordered a brief halt to drone flights after two of its MK30 aircraft collided with a crane outside of Phoenix. No one was injured but the drones sustained substantial damage.
“We’ve completed our own internal review of this incident and are confident that there wasn’t an issue with the drones or the technology that supports them,” Terrence Clark, an Amazon spokesperson, told CNN at the time. “Nonetheless, we’ve introduced additional processes like enhanced visual landscape inspections to better monitor for moving obstructions such as cranes.”
CNN’s Alexandra Skores contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Google alternative Kagi launches an email service
articles.content_orig:
Kagi Mail is launching in public beta with a 60-day free trial.
Kagi Mail is launching in public beta with a 60-day free trial.
Kagi, which already offers a paid alternative to Google Search and its own Orion browser as a rival to Chrome, is taking on another Google service: Gmail. Today, Kagi announced a public beta of Kagi Mail, a new email service that has “no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in.”
With Kagi Mail, you get an @ kagimail.com address, but the service also supports unlimited aliases and domains. It also offers 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar. On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren’t expected to arrive until Q3 2027.
“Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once,” Kagi says. “There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.”
Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial before you have to pay $99 per year. The service is available as part of a $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription.

articles.title_orig: Drone attack on Colombia police base injures civilians, including infant
articles.title_zh: Drone attack on Colombia police base injures civilians, including infant
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is taking aim at Amazon over a warning the online retail giant has been flashing at New Yorkers as they shop: Their orders could soon cost as much as $5 more.
"Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe," Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 19 post on X (1). "It's greed."

Amazon is fighting a proposed New York City law (2) that would overhaul how the company gets packages from its warehouses to your doorstep. And now the giant seems to be recruiting its own customers to help fight that legislative battle.
The company has begun displaying warnings on its website and in its shopping app, directing customers to contact their local lawmakers and oppose the legislation.
For Americans who have come to depend on the convenience of online shopping, the prospect of paying more every time they click "buy" is hardly welcome news. But how much of Amazon's warning should shoppers take at face value?
Introduced in February by New York City Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán, the Delivery Protection Act (3) would require companies operating certain delivery facilities to directly employ most of their warehouse and delivery workers rather than outsource those jobs to third-party contractors.
The legislation would also establish a $500 annual licensing fee per facility, mandatory worker safety training and additional protections against unfair dismissal.
Amazon contends that complying with the legislation could make its existing delivery model economically untenable in New York City, potentially forcing it to relocate operations beyond city limits.
The company has cited research from consulting firm AKRF estimating additional annual household costs of between $409 and $664. However, Amazon hasn't established precisely how those figures translate into a $5 increase per order, per Fox Business (4).
And the bill, which remains in committee, hasn't passed yet.

An extra $5 might seem inconsequential when you're ordering $100 worth of household essentials. But if you order from Amazon twice a week, that potential increase amounts to $520 a year.
A big pill to swallow for Americans caught in escalating financial struggles , especially those already paying $139 annually for Amazon Prime — no doubt in part for its free shipping.
Whether you live in New York City or elsewhere in the country, it's worth taking stock of what you're paying for convenience. Between retail memberships, food delivery subscriptions and expedited shipping, you could be spending hundreds of dollars a year before accounting for the actual goods you're buying.
For retirees living on fixed incomes or workers trying to catch up on their retirement savings, that's money that could be put to better use.
A quick daily check-in of your accounts can show you exactly where your money is going.
An app like Rocket Money can easily flag recurring subscriptions, upcoming bills and unusual charges by pulling in transactions from all your linked accounts.
This can help you cut unnecessary costs so you can manually redirect savings straight into your retirement fund. No spreadsheets, no guesswork, no stress. Small habits like this can make a big difference over time.
Rocket Money's intuitive app offers a variety of free and premium tools. Free features include subscription tracking, bill reminders and budgeting basics, while premium features — like automated savings, net worth tracking, customizable dashboards and more — make it easier to stay on top of your retirement contributions and overall financial goals .
You don't necessarily have to give up online shopping, either. Waiting until you have several items to order, choosing slower shipping when it's cheaper, or picking up your purchases at a nearby store can help trim your expenses.
If those changes free up even $10 a week, consider setting that money aside to build an emergency fund that can cushion your household against future price increases.
A high-yield account like a Wealthfront Cash Account can be a great place to grow your uninvested cash, offering both competitive interest rates and easy access to your money when you need it.

That's about 10 times the national deposit savings rate, according to the FDIC's November report (5).
With no minimum balances or account fees, as well as 24/7 withdrawals and free domestic wire transfers, your funds remain accessible at all times. Plus, you get access to up to $8M FDIC Insurance eligibility through program banks .
When was the last time you compared the price of something on Amazon with what your local retailer charges?
The convenience of having a package arrive at your doorstep tomorrow can make it tempting to skip comparison shopping altogether. And once you've paid for an annual retail membership, you may feel compelled to shop exclusively with that retailer to get your money's worth.
Checking competing retailers' prices, factoring in shipping costs and taking advantage of free in-store pickup could help you keep more of your money.
You can also be more selective about how you pay. If retailers are looking for ways to squeeze a few more dollars out of every transaction, there's no reason you shouldn't try to recover some of that money yourself.
A big chunk of your monthly spending probably goes to the same few things: groceries, gas and a handful of subscriptions. Since you're paying for them anyway, putting those routine purchases on a cash back credit card is one way to get some of that money back.
Many cards pay higher cash back in select categories like these. Say you spend $500 a month on groceries and gas and earn 3% back in those categories. That's $180 a year for purchases you'd make anyway.
Just keep in mind that rewards only pay off if you clear your balance each month. Card balances that carry interest averaged a 22.36% APR in August, according to the Federal Reserve, and at that rate, interest can quickly cancel out what you earn.
Some of these cards come with extra perks, too. Many offer a welcome bonus once you hit a minimum spend in the first few months, and some pay higher cash back in select categories like groceries, gas or dining. A big purchase you were already planning could help you reach that bonus faster. Shop around to find a 0% intro APR card with perks that fit your spending habits.

articles.title_orig: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.title_zh: Congress reacts with anger and skepticism about Jensen Huang reinstatement
articles.content_orig:
The stock market was thrilled with the announcement that Jensen Huang was returning as CEO of Nvidia, but lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with shock — and said they still expect him to answer questions next week on Capitol Hill .
“You gotta be kidding me,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told MS NOW when he learned of Huang’s reinstatement 11 days after he resigned in the wake of revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese spy.
In its announcement, the board said it reached the decision after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
“No national security risk? Based on what?” Cornyn asked in a post on X .
President Donald Trump told CNBC he’d spoken to the board “directly and indirectly.”
“One of the things the board wanted to know, is there a national security problem?” Trump said. “And after a lot of research, we — you know, we’ve been looking at this for more than a couple of days, right? This has been a story for a few weeks. We said no, it’s not a problem.”
Lawmakers made clear they still need answers.
The Senate Banking Committee, chaired by Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced that Huang was scheduled to testify publicly Dec. 3.
“The national security concerns and adherence to export controls will be central to the committee’s oversight and the congressional hearing. Our markets demand transparency. Americans deserve the truth. Our committee will deliver answers,” Scott said in a statement.
A spokesperson for the House Intelligence Committee told NBC News that Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with Huang on Dec. 1.
“There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
In a joint statement later Monday, the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, the Intelligence Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee said Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter “have confirmed they will appear for their transcribed interviews on December 1 and December 2 as previously planned.”
“We remain committed to getting answers on the mass smuggling of NVIDIA products, their diversion for Chinese military purposes, and their key role in advancing our foremost adversary’s AI capabilities,” said the three Republicans, Reps. John Moolenaar of Michigan, Rick Crawford of Arkansas and Brian Mast of Florida.
The speedy reinstatement and assurances of the lack of a security risk came after the Justice and Commerce departments last week shared details about their investigation into Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang , the suspected spy with whom Huang was allegedly involved.
Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said in an X post that “the legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now born by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens. The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., told NBC News in a phone interview “It’s not my job as a public official to tell a private company who to pick for their CEO. That’s up to the board of directors.”
But, he added, “What I want to know is whether Nvidia violated the export controls of our country with respect to advanced chips. And I want to know if the Department of Commerce did. That will be the purpose of the Banking Committee hearing.”
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said in a statement that the administration appears to have known about the Chinese espionage efforts targeting the Nvidia CEO for the past year and his reinstatement “without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the administration’s “rush to reinstate Jensen Huang underscores the need for Congress to act.”
“Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasizing that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said in a statement. He added that “Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.”
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., called the board’s decision “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”
“Congress will not be deterred from conducting a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation into business malfeasance by NVIDIA and corrupt abuse of power by Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce,” Jeffries said.
Lutnick agreed earlier this month to testify before Congress about the Huang scandal amid lawmakers’ scrutiny of China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Democrats pointed Trump’s financial ties to Nvidia, with Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking member on the Oversight Committee, noting the president has a sizeable amount of Nvidia stock. “No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions,” Garcia said .
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., cited Nvidia’s donation to Trump’s White House ballroom project as a reason to give the board’s decision extra scrutiny.
“Trump’s assurances cannot be taken at face value, especially after Nvidia’s $25 million donation to his ballroom. Huang must testify at a full public congressional hearing, with every member of the relevant committees allowed to question him,” he posted on X.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., questioned the Nvidia board’s decision in a post on social media.
“Jensen Huang had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy,” Ricketts wrote. “His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement.”
“Nvidia’s decision today doesn’t excuse Jensen Huang from testifying before Congress,” he continued. “It also doesn’t absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips. I look forward to Mr. Huang coming to the Senate in December.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., called the president’s actions “Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration’s big tech and AI policy.” He told reporters it was a “good sign” that Republican senators and lawmakers have spoken out because they “realize this is a threat to national security.”
Dareh Gregorian is a politics reporter for NBC News.
Brennan Leach is an associate producer for NBC News covering the Senate.

articles.title_orig: Republicans Break With Trump Over Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement at Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Republicans Break With Trump Over Jensen Huang’s Reinstatement at Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

articles.title_orig: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.
The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.
When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.
Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s return as it happened: Nvidia gains nearly $1tn in value after co-founder reinstated
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s return as it happened: Nvidia gains nearly $1tn in value after co-founder reinstated
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang and Donald Trump on Sept. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Eleven days. That’s how long it took Jensen Huang to return to his post of CEO of Nvidia after resigning in the wake of an alleged espionage scandal that rocked the business, tech, and policy worlds.
On Nov. 12, Huang stepped down from the company he co-founded in 1993 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected was a Chinese spy. Her former company, Megaspeed, is also under criminal investigation over possible export-control violations. (The two Huangs are not related.)
But on Monday, Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his reinstatement “poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump personally claimed credit for the reversal, telling CNBC that “I convinced them” and “I made the deal.”
The stock market surged, with Nvidia shares rising more than 30% as trading opened Monday. The broader market has now recovered more than half of last week’s plunge, temporarily easing fears that an AI slump could lead to a recession.
But Nvidia and Huang still face an uncertain and treacherous path forward. Here are six big questions about his return.
Just a week ago, the NVIDIA board made it clear that it intended to turn the page on the Huang era. At the company’s Q3 earnings call on Nov. 17, chairman Harvey Jones told investors that the board did “not intend to reinstate Huang,” despite the fact that the former CEO was angling for a return.
The board had plenty of reasons to not want him back. Reuters reported that Huang had misled several company leaders about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Separate reports emerged alleging that Jensen Huang had relationships with two Nvidia employees, including Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reported to him.
But the board also faced intense pressure to reinstate him. An online campaign attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including from executives like Elon Musk and people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees.
And most centrally, President Trump said Monday that he personally intervened. Trump told CNBC that he had spoken to Nvidia’s board “directly and indirectly,” and that Vice President JD Vance was also involved in discussions. On Monday morning, Trump indicated to a reporter that he knew Huang would be reinstated before the news broke.
Notably, the board reinstated Huang before completing its independent investigation. Directors said a series of meetings had satisfied them about Huang’s “candor and ability to lead,” and that senior government officials had assuaged their national-security concerns. They did not identify those officials or explain what information they supplied.
The swift about-face has provoked questions even from Republicans. "Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” wrote Utah Senator John Curtis.
It remains unclear what U.S. intelligence discovered about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang—and how damaging its findings were. The New York Times reported Sunday that Alice Huang remained in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 through the fall of 2026—a period overlapping with her affair with Jensen Huang.
But the intelligence community has not publicly established that she knowingly acted as a spy, and Beijing has denied the allegation. Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday that Attorney General Todd Blanche did “not possess evidence” that Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
However, a slew of questions remains unanswered. Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, said on Sunday that an investigation into Alice Huang and her firm Megaspeed was ongoing. And more reporting continues to be published about the complex relationships between Megaspeed, the Chinese government, and various Chinese AI companies. Bloomberg, for instance, reported that a company founded by Alice Huang procured Nvidia chips installed at a Shanghai data center connected to the Megaspeed network.
The Nvidia scandal has exacerbated deep fissures within the Trump administration over China. More laissez-faire members of the administration, exemplified by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are happy with Nvidia selling some of its chips to China, which they argue is good for U.S. business interests and keeping China hooked on American technology.
But the Nvidia scandal empowered a competing faction of China hawks, who argue that Trump should take a more adversarial stance. Four days after Huang resigned, the Commerce Department issued a rule intended to close a major loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access restricted American chips remotely through data centers in third countries.
With Huang back in charge at Nvidia, the balance could tip back in his favor.
The scandal has also revealed cracks within Nvidia, the world’s top chip supplier. It’s no secret that Huang has always been the culture-setter for Nvidia and its hard-charging, relentless work ethic. But recent reporting, especially from the Times , alleges that Huang crossed a line into public humiliation, threats, and verbal abuse.
Now that Huang is back, will his power be checked—or unleashed? The board, in its statement, stressed more oversight, including a new committee of independent directors that will oversee national-security and export-control risks, and a chief compliance officer who reports to a board committee.
But Huang has now survived a seemingly insurmountable crisis with the support of the president and other Silicon Valley power players. That could make him more difficult to restrain, in a manner similar to how Sam Altman returned to OpenAI with a reconstituted board that left him more powerful than before his ouster.
Lindsey Stewart, director of institutional insights at Morningstar, an investment research company, says that the fact that Huang was reinstated before his investigation was concluded “is going to add to those corporate governance questions that investors have"—especially given that the company is "exposed to several material risks."
As Huang resumes the role of helming one of the biggest companies in the world, he will also be pulled away from his desk to Washington to answer questions from irate policymakers. He has agreed to a transcribed congressional interview on Dec. 1 before the House Intelligence, Foreign Affairs, and China committees, and has also been asked to appear on Dec. 3 in a public Senate hearing.
That scrutiny will likely increase in January, when Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. Many Democratic candidates ran on platforms of accountability and rooting out corruption. Lawmakers have already demanded that the administration preserve records involving Nvidia, Megaspeed, Huang’s communications with Trump, and the government’s export-control decisions.
“Congress must get to the bottom of what’s going on at Nvidia. Jensen Huang must testify under oath,” Congressman Greg Casar wrote in a statement on Monday.
Investigators may also examine Trump’s financial interest in Nvidia. Public disclosures show that he bought between $1 million and $5 million of Nvidia stock in the days before his administration rescinded a Biden-era chip rule in May 2025, and made at least three additional purchases shortly after announcing that Nvidia could sell H200 chips to China. White House representatives have stated that Trump’s holdings are managed by independent advisors.
Huang’s return stopped the stock market bleeding on Monday. Longterm, his presence could be enormously beneficial to an industry that critics feared was on the verge of bursting. Huang has long played the role of AI’s chief investor, salesman, and diplomat.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.title_zh: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
articles.content_orig:
Art: Arina Istomina / Mediazona
By the end of September 2026, at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in the war with Ukraine. These are people whose deaths have already been officially registered and appear in data leaked from a hack of Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, shared with the journalists by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers (Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow).
We are confident that this data is genuine. It holds up against our named list of the military dead (including entries not yet published), the national Probate Registry, other leaked civil registry databases, publicly available court rulings, and Rosstat’s own previously published statistics.
The Rosstat files also allowed us to double-check our earlier casualty estimates based on the Probate Registry—showing that those estimates were largely accurate, or even conservative when it comes to soldiers missing in action.
Accounting for delays in death registration, we estimate that the true number of Russian military dead stood at around 700,000 as of September.
This is a joint report with Meduza as part of our war mortality estimation project. The named list of the Russian military dead is compiled by Mediazona, the BBC’s Russian service, and a team of volunteers.
Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow announced their breach of Rosstat on November 1. They gained access not only to the agency’s website but also to its internal networks, exfiltrating terabytes of files—including mortality data that Rosstat stopped publishing in mid-2025. On November 8, the hackers shared the data with journalists.
Along with other media outlets, we received a database containing 29.7 million records, covering nearly all death registrations in Russia’s Unified State Register of Civil Status Records (EGR ZAGS) from the start of 2021 through August 2026. Rosstat receives these records in anonymised form: each entry includes demographic details, but no name.
On November 15, the hackers passed journalists a second batch of files: 15 million newer records from SMEV—Russia’s Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction System—covering death registrations through September 29, 2026. Outlets that published mortality figures based on the first leak only had access to data through August, which is why some published counts may differ.
The raw files contained multiple versions of the same death record, duplicates, and subsequent amendments, making data cleaning a nontrivial task. After processing both databases and removing errors and duplicates, we arrived at 11,658,178 unique death records. This total may still contain a small number of duplicates—for instance, where entries are incomplete or contain errors.
The raw mortality data comes from three sources. The first is a copy of a Rosstat MongoDB database called “deathFacts”, which stores anonymised death records. The hackers obtained this during their initial breach of Rosstat’s internal network, and its records run through early August 2026. The second is a separate dump from the same database accumulated while the hackers retained network access, though it only captures deaths through the end of August. The third source is a copy of a PostgreSQL database from the Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction System (SMEV), which continued receiving death records until the hackers lost access at the end of September 2026.
SMEV is the channel through which Rosstat receives already anonymised “raw” entries from the Unified State Register (EGR), which holds all vital records filed by Russian civil registry offices. Transfers to Rosstat via SMEV began in June 2023; prior to that, Rosstat appears to have received monthly spreadsheets separately from each region. Once SMEV was introduced, Rosstat’s internal database began populating automatically, with records undergoing additional processing—certain fields were stripped out while blank ones were filled in. For example, if the exact day of death was left blank in SMEV, Rosstat populated it with either the first of the month or the registration date of the death record itself.
Taken together, this gave us 29.7 million records in MongoDB from 2021 to late August 2026 (only around 100,000 entries date from earlier years) and 15 million “raw” records from June 2023 to late September 2026.
These entries do not correspond one-to-one with unique deaths: almost every death has multiple versions. In most cases, new versions reflect updated details or filled-in fields, such as a refined cause of death or previously missing dates. MongoDB contains roughly 11.7 million unique record numbers, while SMEV contains 6.7 million.
We retained only the latest active version of each record, which is typically the most complete. Occasionally, a record has no active version and its final entry is marked as revoked; we found about 286,000 such cases. This usually means the death was entered outside the official “reporting period” and excluded from published statistics. In 23,000 cases, we matched the revoked entry to a replacement record using dates of birth and death, birthplace, or death certificate number. In the remaining 263,000 cases, we kept the revoked version as evidence of a unique death.
The two databases overlap substantially: SMEV adds around 210,000 new death records and 60,000 updated versions of records already present in MongoDB.
In principle, every death registration carries a unique 21-digit vital record number following a strict format. The first digit denotes the EGR section (always 1 for vital records). The second denotes the record type—birth, marriage, divorce, death, etc. (7 for deaths). The next three digits encode the registration year; the following eight identify the civil registry office or issuing authority; and the next five give the sequential number for that record type at that office within the year (the first death recorded there in a given year is 00001). Digits 19 and 20 denote an “additional attribute,” and the final digit is a check digit.
“Additional attributes” describe the circumstances under which a record was created—such as digitising a paper record or entering a death while offline. As a result, the same death can end up sharing a sequential number while carrying a different 21-digit ID that differs only in the final three digits (the additional attribute and check digit). We merged records with identical 18-digit prefixes, matching dates of birth and death, and matching sex: 375,000 entries consolidated into 152,000 unique deaths (usually two or three versions of one death, and four in a single case).
In practice, however, civil registry offices sometimes issue two separate original records (coded 00 in the additional attribute) under the same sequential number. When entered into the online system, one may be assigned a different code, such as 10. In those cases, two completely different deaths share everything except the last three digits. In Rosstat’s database, we even found different individuals recorded under the exact same ID across different versions of a single record. In some instances we located new record numbers for these “overwritten” entries, but in roughly 1,000 cases we had to retain two distinct deaths under the same record number.
We also merged duplicates where the same death was re-registered at a different civil registry office—something that happened on a large scale with deaths initially registered in Rostov offices or declared by court ruling. On its own, the combination of date of birth and date of death identifies an individual fairly well: most pairs appear once or twice, very rarely five times, and more often only in isolated cases (typically when incomplete dates default to the first of the month or year). Any single additional matching field—birthplace, death certificate number (allowing for a one-character typo), place of death, or name where known—establishes an unambiguous match. articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang went to war with Washington — and won a path to China
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang went to war with Washington — and won a path to China
articles.content_orig:
For a minute there, it seemed like someone in the Trump administration might actually be willing to stand up to China.
For about a week and a half, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was the face of an emerging harder line on Nvidia over the potential risks its co-founder Jensen Huang 's affairs posed to national security. Bessent was giving voice to China hawks who had felt sidelined by the Trump administration's willingness to sell artificial intelligence chips to  China.
They see China's AI program as a major threat, and want to restrain its growth by cutting off the supply of advanced chips to China. The resignation of Huang, who pressed the Trump Administration to allow the exports, seemed to signal that the hawks had found new influence in Washington.
By this weekend, Bessent had softened his public resistance to Huang's reinstatement. That came just in time for Nvidia's board to reappoint Huang as CEO at President Donald Trump 's urging.
Whether any real damage was done to national security isn't clear. But it is safe to say that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress won't take Trump at his word when he said on CNBC Monday that the Department of Justice "did a pretty good investigation" that exonerated Huang.
Congress will look deeply into the worries Bessent himself raised about Huang's acknowledged romantic relationship with a woman The New York Times and others have reported was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia's board said it had received assurances from top U.S. officials and had concluded his return wasn't a national security risk.
A top concern is whether China was able to use the affair to help divert Nvidia's high-end artificial intelligence chips toward helping its military. Bessent in a Nov. 13 interview with CNBC outlined the stakes.
"Any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts the — it hurts our great companies and in the AI race it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Bessent said that his department and others had wanted to blacklist Megaspeed, the company previously run by Alice Huang, Jensen Huang's paramour. But "Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.
The Commerce Department is headed by Secretary Howard Lutnick, Bessent's rival.
Putting Huang back at Nvidia wasn't originally Bessent's preference. He said in a Fox interview on Nov. 15 that the board should "go outside the company" to find a new leader. But by this past weekend, Bessent had apparently gotten on board with Trump's wishes.
"Jensen is on the outside now," Bessent told CBS on Sunday, in trying to explain his apparent policy shift.
Commerce has since taken steps to tighten some restrictions meant to prevent U.S. chips from helping China advance in the AI race.
But there is bipartisan worry about the Nvidia episode. "I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done," Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., told The Wall Street Journal . He said Lutnick had not responded to letters he sent saying the administration should be "taking the threats of communist China more seriously."
But Trump has clearly put an upper limit on how aggressively anyone in his administration can push back on China. The president said Monday that he was swayed by the pageantry in his visit to China last week.
Xi "met me at the plane, which is something they've never done, which was a sign," Trump said.
Trump said he felt like he needed to intervene to back Huang because the stock market was plummeting in the wake of Nvidia's troubles — a development he also blamed on Democrats' midterm victory.
"I watched our country lose $5 trillion because of a bad election," he said. "If I didn't get involved, you'd probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come." Now, its stock performance will be "unbelievable."
Bessent on Sunday played down the market risks. The company "continues to be fantastically profitable, and there is near unlimited demand for their chips worldwide," he told CBS.
Lutnick has embraced Trump's transactional urges. He has backed deals in which the U.S. takes equity stakes in companies such as Intel, saying the taxpayer deserves some of the upside.
Lutnick in January said he had heard Huang pitch Trump on allowing Nvidia to sell its relatively more advanced H200 chips into China.
"There are strong — two sides. We shouldn't sell them any or we should sell them." Where does he stand? "Right in the middle," Lutnick told Bloomberg . Trump decided to go ahead with the deal.
Bessent has said he is "neither a hawk nor a dove" on China, and is simply trying to manage the ultra-sensitive relationship between the world's two biggest economies. But the upshot of the Huang affair seems to be that Bessent wasn't able to sway the president on a matter that seemed cut-and-dried just days ago.
Lutnick, meanwhile, is riding high.
Trump said he discussed whether Huang should return to Nvidia with Lutnick, Bessent and Vice President JD Vance. "Howard Lutnick was very good. Very, he's very professional," Trump said on CNBC Monday.
"I call them the opposites, Scott and Howard," Trump added, before declaring them "both good."

articles.title_orig: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.title_zh: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
articles.content_orig:
Looking for a web browser without Google Chrome underneath? You can try this independent web browser now on macOS and Linux.
Looking for a web browser without Google Chrome underneath? You can try this independent web browser now on macOS and Linux.
Ladybird, an independent web browser with a built-from-scratch engine, is finally available for testing. On Monday, Ladybird developer Andreas Kling announced that the browser is launching in alpha on macOS and Linux following more than four years of development.
The release makes Ladybird the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new engine. We’ve seen many engines emerge over time, but the most popular browsers use just three today: Gecko, Blink, and WebKit. While Gecko, now used in Mozilla Firefox, first appeared in Netscape 6 in 2000 , Apple’s WebKit arrived in Safari in 2003 as a fork of KDE’s KHTML. A decade later, the Google-backed Chromium project forked WebKit to create Blink, which now powers Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera, and more.
Ladybird is backed by a nonprofit organization with the goal of creating “an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web,” according to its website . Though Ladybird development initially began as part of a C++ project, its developers eventually began porting the code to Rust using AI .
In his post announcing the alpha, Kling notes that the browser built around the Ladybird engine “is modest but functional,” adding that “some websites won’t work” during the alpha. A Windows version of Ladybird will arrive during a “later stage” of the project.

articles.title_orig: Trump made up to $15mn on Nvidia shares after Huang’s return
articles.title_zh: Trump made up to $15mn on Nvidia shares after Huang’s return
articles.content_orig:
The president has said that it’s critical for U.S. to win the AI race with China, but he has downplayed espionage allegations about China obtaining advanced chips from Nvidia.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly brushed off concerns about China’s aggressive spying on the U.S., which the Nvidia scandal shows has reached some of the highest levels of America’s most sensitive industries.
To the president, China is just doing what everyone else does, including Washington. “I think we spy better than they do,” Trump said in an interview last week on Fox News while in Shenzhen. “We spy on China, they spy on us.”
But former intelligence officials and lawmakers in both parties say otherwise.
The president’s stance is now being tested by a scandal at the center of the U.S. artificial intelligence industry. Trump personally intervened over the weekend to persuade Nvidia, the world’s leading producer of advanced AI chips, to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.
Huang was ousted earlier this month after two extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer accused of routing advanced AI chips to Chinese companies in possible violation of U.S. export controls.
Current and former national security officials are alarmed by the Huang saga because of Nvidia’s central place in the AI race between Washington and Beijing. The U.S. has tried for years to keep its most advanced AI chips, the hardware used to train and run cutting-edge models, out of China’s hands. The New York Times reported that Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen restrictions on selling Nvidia chips to China.
Trump missed an opportunity while in China last week to raise Washington’s concerns about Beijing’s espionage and influence operations, analysts said.
“We’re not taking any retaliatory moves, and what that says to the Chinese is everything is fair game now,” said Dennis Wilder, a former head of China analysis at the CIA and a top White House Asia adviser during the George W. Bush administration. “Giving them a pass just means they’ll do a whole lot more.”
The U.S. has a host of concerns with Chinese spying, including theft of American technology, malicious cyber activity and covert efforts to influence U.S. politics and public opinion. The FBI calls confronting China’s intelligence gathering and economic espionage its “top counterintelligence priority.”
“They are one of the world’s most aggressive intelligence services, and they bring a lot of resources to bear,” said Emily Harding, director of the intelligence, national security and technology program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “They don’t really see a line between a government employee and a Chinese citizen abroad that could do them a favor.”
Trump’s dismissal of Chinese activity weakens the U.S. ability to try to set a baseline, Wilder said, adding that there are different levels of spying behavior, many governed by gentleman’s agreements.
“Trump is giving a picture of equal behavior, and China’s behavior is far beyond the bounds of just legitimate espionage,” Wilder said.
Trump posted on Truth Social Monday that the U.S. “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to national security.”
While there is much more to be learned about Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the avalanche of revelations in recent weeks has prompted lawmakers of both parties to open investigations into the company and to press the administration to do more to confront China.
“We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology,” said Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., a former CIA analyst, said Huang’s reinstatement raised “deeply serious questions about Chinese Communist Party influence.”
Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Select Committee on China, said Trump’s attitude toward China and Nvidia was hurting U.S. interests.
“I’m deeply concerned about whether he and Nvidia knowingly violated export control laws, and we have a bipartisan hearing that we plan to get to the bottom of these issues,” he told MS NOW in an interview.
“What we see is an unholy alliance between wealth and power that is compromising American national security,” he said.
The expanding espionage and extramarital-affair scandal around Jensen Huang loomed large over Trump’s China trip. Trump said he spoke to Chinese President Xi Jinping about the Nvidia CEO “at length” but did not raise American concerns with Xi that Alice Huang was a spy or working with China’s intelligence service, the Ministry of State Security.
“He really doesn’t know much about him, other than he is a brilliant man,” Trump told CNBC on Monday.
Peggy Helman and Julianne McShane contributed reporting.
Felicia Schwartz is a national security reporter for MS NOW.

articles.title_orig: Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia sparks fury in Congress as lawmakers move forward with hearings
articles.title_zh: Huang's reinstatement at Nvidia sparks fury in Congress as lawmakers move forward with hearings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said to expect "a stronger hearing than normal" when lawmakers have a chance to grill now-reinstated Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang next week.
"What I want to know is the exact tick-tock of how this all occurred," Gallego said, listing questions such as when Huang learned about suspicions of his paramour's involvement with Chinese intelligence, and whether he purposely helped her company evade a ban on semiconductor exports, as well as President Trump's involvement.
"I think it does bring sharper questions into focus," he added.
Gallego spoke to Yahoo Finance on Monday shortly after the Senate Banking Committee, where Gallego sits as a member, confirmed that Jensen's testimony will go forward on Dec. 3 .
Gallego's comments underscore the battle Huang will face in Washington in the months ahead, despite having Trump's backing .
Many lawmakers, even in Trump's own party, are not fully on board with Huang's reinstatement. Hard questions in the hearing a week from Thursday are likely to come from both sides of the aisle.
Another member of the panel, Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, posted on X Monday, listing issues dogging Huang, such as his reported multiple affairs and lack of "candor" with his own board of directors.
"His behavior does not support reinstatement," Ricketts wrote.
Gallego's comments were part of a flurry from Democrats who quickly promised aggressive oversight when they take power in January.
"Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives," Chuck Schumer, the likely Senate majority leader, wrote on X .
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate's banking panel and in line to take over in 2027, said in a statement in which she called Huang's reinstatement "a reckless decision."
Gallego — who is mentioned as a possible 2028 presidential candidate — said he also wants to hear from members of Nvidia's board of directors, as well as officials at the Commerce Department who ran the semiconductor export control program, whom he called "the executioners of this."
He said he is keenly interested in whether the president or members of his team, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, profited from Nvidia's gyrating stock or previous loopholes in semiconductor exports.
Gallego and his colleagues will also likely have a second opportunity to probe these issues with Lutnick, who has agreed to testify publicly , potentially on Dec. 10.
Gallego said he expects that Lutnick will appear, noting that if he tried to avoid testifying in 2026, he would face a Congress in 2027 with Democrats in control.
In that case, Gallego said, "I think he's going to find himself in a worse situation."
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.content_orig:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.
“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.
“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
The Board also recently formed a National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging counsel with experience in national security matters, and such counsel will be retaining advisors with expertise in national security matters. NVIDIA is commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer, to oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries.

articles.title_orig: Cocaine Gangs Batter Colombian Security Forces in Wave of Attacks
articles.title_zh: Cocaine Gangs Batter Colombian Security Forces in Wave of Attacks
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.
Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.
Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.
The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.
Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.
Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.
In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.
However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.
Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.
Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street Storms Back as AI Trade Rebounds With Huang’s Return
articles.title_zh: Wall Street Storms Back as AI Trade Rebounds With Huang’s Return
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street spent last week dumping anything tied to AI. It spent Monday buying it back.
The Invesco QQQ Trust ( QQQ ), the fund that tracks the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ), opened almost 8% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 1999. Its closest rivals for largest jumps came in 2000 and 2001 as the dot-com bubble was bursting and big rallies had a habit of fizzling.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) opened 5% higher. Among Mondays since 1993, only Oct. 13, 2008, in the depths of the financial crisis, started with a bigger jump.
The rally held. The S&P 500 closed up nearly 5% for its best day since April 2025, the Nasdaq 100 jumped almost 7% and the CBOE Volatility Index ( ^VIX ) fell more than 9 points.
The surge came as Nvidia ( NVDA ) brought back Jensen Huang as CEO , and after the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slid into a correction last week.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) opened 15% higher, its biggest jump at the open since it launched in 2001 and well past its previous record of about 9% in October 2002.
Nvidia opened up 33% on Huang's return and closed up about 31%, its third-best day ever, behind only March 2000 and May 2003. Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), Micron ( MU ) and AMD ( AMD ) closed roughly 7% to 19% higher.
Read more: Buy Nvidia stock or wait? A guide to making the call on any stock.
Not everyone thinks the panic has run its course. Options sentiment "screams" the worst levels since the pandemic and Liberation Day, Roundhill Investments chief investment strategist Drew Pettit told Yahoo Finance, "but it's not a washout."
History sides with the bulls, eventually. In the 20 times since 1993 that SPY opened Monday 2% or more higher, it was higher a year later in 17 of those, with a median gain of about 25%, roughly double that of a typical year, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Creative Planning's Charlie Bilello found a similar pattern . Last week's nearly 9% drop was the S&P 500's 12th-worst week since 1950, he noted, and after the worst weeks, stocks averaged a 26% gain over the next year, compared with 11% otherwise.
Evercore ISI's Julian Emanuel is in that camp too, writing over the weekend, "Bull Market intact as double-digit EPS gains likely ahead."
In half of those 20 cases, SPY slipped back below the prior Friday's low within three months, most often within two weeks. Think of it as the morning after a big night out. The headache usually comes back before it goes away.
Even so, eight of those 10 were higher a year later. The two closest matches to this setup, October 2008 and May 2010, each paired a brutal week with a big Monday open, sank further over the next three months and were about 15% higher a year later.
That puts Friday's low, about 6,883 on the S&P 500, in focus. And the Fed isn't riding to the rescue , with Wall Street still pricing a December rate hike and every correction that hits with inflation speeding up this fast turning into a bear market .
BTIG's strategists aren't calling a bottom yet. "We don't think this is the final low, but we are looking for a short-term rally back towards 7250-7350 before likely turning lower again," they wrote over the weekend.
The S&P 500 finished Monday just shy of that range.

articles.title_orig: US moves to recover over $1B in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in Binance heist
articles.title_zh: US moves to recover over $1B in crypto stolen by North Korean hackers in Binance heist
articles.content_orig:
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng tells FOX Business' Darren Botelho that customers will not bear any losses following a massive $6.3B hack. Teng emphasizes that the cryptocurrency exchange bears full responsibility and has replenished affected assets.
The U.S. government has begun legal proceedings to recover more than $1 billion in cryptocurrency stolen by North Korean hackers during a $6 billion heist from the Binance crypto exchange.
So far, the government has helped seize and freeze more than $3 billion of the stolen digital assets, the Justice Department said Monday. The legal action targets all USDC—a stablecoin issued by Circle Internet Financial, LLC—held across 36 virtual currency addresses spanning 18 different blockchain networks.
"Today’s action speaks to the speed and lengths that we in the U.S. government will go to stop sophisticated cybercriminals," said Jeanine Ferris Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia. "Whether it is a lone hacker or an enemy nation-state, and wherever the criminal proceeds may go, my office and our partners will meet the moment, go toe-to-toe with our adversaries, and help victims of crime."
EXPERT WARNS OF 'AI HACKING BLOODBATH' FOLLOWING MASSIVE BINANCE CRYPTOCURRENCY THEFT
The Treasury Department says North Korea has used overseas IT workers operating under false identities to generate revenue for the regime's weapons programs. On Oct. 29, North Korean hackers stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, (Budrul Chukrut/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)
North Korean hackers breached Binance’s internal network and hot wallets on Oct. 29, making off with roughly $6 billion in virtual currency.
The breach originated from a social engineering scheme targeting a company employee, according to an internal probe by Binance.
NORTH KOREA RESPONSIBLE FOR $6 BILLION BINANCE CRYPTOCURRENCY HACK, FBI SAYS
Richard Teng, chief executive officer of Binance, during the DC Blockchain Summit in Washington, D.C., on March 26, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
A purported job recruiter contacted the employee, who expressed interest in the role and agreed to an interview, according to court documents. During the interview process, the employee was instructed to download software that was secretly laced with malware .
"Unbeknownst to the Binance employee, that software contained malware. The employee’s compromised device allowed the criminal actors to install an EIP-7702 injection on the device," the complaint states.
Eric Schiffer, chairman of Patriarch and Reputation Management Consultants, warns that the $6.3 billion Binance hack could signal a wave of cyberattacks.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Following the heist, the hackers have continued attempting to launder the stolen funds through cryptocurrency exchanges, bridges and mixing services designed to obscure the movement of digital assets, FOX Business previously reported.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng previously told FOX Business that the company closed the entry points exploited by the hackers and rebuilt the affected systems.
FOX Business' Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.
